city.name: Saigon
summary: Saigon was the capital of South Vietnam, a city of about three million by 1975 on the Saigon River. The French had laid out its centre as a colonial capital, with a cathedral, a post office, an opera house and tree-lined boulevards; by the 1960s concrete hotels and offices had risen among them. To the south-west lay Cholon, the crowded Chinese twin city of shophouses and markets.

During the Tet Offensive, early on 31 January 1968, Viet Cong squads struck the US Embassy, the presidential palace, the radio station and the Tan Son Nhut air base. The attacks in the centre were beaten off within hours, but fighting in Cholon lasted for weeks.

In April 1975 North Vietnamese divisions closed in on the city. On 29 and 30 April US helicopters lifted Americans and South Vietnamese from the Defense Attaché Office at Tan Son Nhut and from the embassy roof to ships offshore. At about 11:00 on 30 April a tank broke through the gates of Independence Palace and the government surrendered.
city.note: Streets are today's from OpenStreetMap, kept only in the old centre, Da Kao, Cholon and the road to Tan Son Nhut; they are labelled with their names of 1975 where those are known to have changed. The river and canals are today's OpenStreetMap water: the waterfront quays have been rebuilt since. Landmark outlines come from OpenStreetMap where the building survives; the US Embassy, demolished in 1998, is placed by its address at 4 Thong Nhat Boulevard with an approximate outline. Houses between the streets are generated, and only for the inner districts: the rest of the city, built up to the air base by 1975, is shown by its streets alone. properties.name: Independence Palace
description: The presidential palace of South Vietnam, built from 1962 to 1966 by the architect Ngo Viet Thu on the site of the French governors' Norodom Palace, which two rebel pilots had bombed in 1962. Its screen of concrete fins was meant to recall bamboo. Nguyen Van Thieu lived and worked here from 1967 until he resigned on 21 April 1975.

Viet Cong sappers attacked its gates at Tet in 1968 and were driven off. On 8 April 1975 a South Vietnamese pilot who was a communist agent bombed it from an F-5. At about 11:00 on 30 April a North Vietnamese T-54 broke through the main gate; President Duong Van Minh, in office for two days, surrendered here that afternoon.

properties.name: Main gate
properties.description: Tank 390 of the North Vietnamese 203rd Armoured Brigade crashed through these iron gates at about 11:00 on 30 April 1975; tank 843, ahead of it, had jammed against the side gate. A soldier ran up to the palace roof and raised the flag of the Provisional Revolutionary Government.

properties.name: US Embassy
properties.wiki: Embassy of the United States, Saigon
description: A six-storey chancery on Thong Nhat Boulevard, opened in September 1967, wrapped in a white concrete screen against bombs and with a small helipad on the roof.

At 02:45 on 31 January 1968, 19 Viet Cong sappers blew a hole in the compound wall and fought in the grounds until the embassy was declared secure at 09:00. 18 of them were killed and one captured; four US military policemen and a Marine died. The attackers never entered the building, but the images shocked Americans who had been told the war was being won.

On 29 April 1975 some 2,500 evacuees were inside the embassy and consular compounds and about 10,000 people were gathered outside. Through the night helicopters lifted people from the roof and from the car park, cleared of its trees as a landing zone. Ambassador Graham Martin left at 04:58 on 30 April; the last Marines were taken off the roof at 07:53, leaving some 400 evacuees behind. The building was demolished in 1998.

properties.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
properties.description: The cathedral of Saigon, built from 1877 to 1880 of red brick shipped from Toulouse. Its two towers, 57 m high, were added in 1895.

properties.name: Central Post Office
properties.description: The post office of 1886 to 1891 by Alfred Foulhoux, often wrongly credited to Gustave Eiffel, with a vaulted iron hall inside and painted maps of the telegraph lines of Cochinchina.

properties.name: Hotel Continental
properties.description: Saigon's oldest hotel, opened in 1880 at the corner of Rue Catinat and the square by the opera house. Its terrace was a meeting place for journalists and officials, and the setting of Graham Greene's The Quiet American.

properties.name: Caravelle Hotel
properties.description: A ten-storey hotel opened on Christmas Eve 1959, then the tallest building in Saigon. News bureaus and the Australian embassy had offices in it, and reporters watched the war's flares and fires from its rooftop bar. A bomb exploded on the fifth floor, used by foreign journalists, on 25 August 1964.

properties.name: Lower House (Opera House)
properties.wiki: Ho Chi Minh City Opera House
properties.description: The Opera House of 1900. From 1956 it housed South Vietnam's National Assembly, and from 1967 its Lower House.

properties.name: City Hall (Hôtel de Ville)
properties.description: The Hôtel de Ville, opened in 1909 at the head of Nguyen Hue boulevard, with its clock tower.

properties.name: Rex Hotel
properties.description: The US military command held its daily press briefings here, which reporters who doubted their optimism called the Five O'Clock Follies.

properties.name: Ben Thanh market
properties.description: The central market, in its iron and concrete halls of 1912 to 1914 with a clock tower over the south gate.

properties.name: Tu Do Street (Rue Catinat)
properties.description: The Rue Catinat of the French, renamed Tu Do (Freedom) Street in 1955 and Dong Khoi (Uprising) after 1975: the city's smartest street, running from the cathedral down to the river past the Continental and the Caravelle, lined with bars and shops that served the American soldiers and press.

properties.name: Cholon
description: The 'big market', Saigon's Chinese twin city, a dense grid of shophouses, temples, rice mills and markets along the canals.

At Tet in 1968 Viet Cong battalions used the Phu Tho racecourse nearby as a base, and fighting in Cholon went on house by house into February. In May 1968 a second wave of attacks hit Cholon again; four Australian journalists were killed there.

properties.name: Binh Tay market
properties.description: Cholon's largest market, built in 1928 to 1930 round a courtyard, with Chinese tiled roofs and a clock tower.

properties.name: Phu Tho racecourse
properties.description: A racecourse on the edge of Cholon, which Viet Cong units seized at Tet in 1968 as a staging area and command post. US and South Vietnamese troops drove them out after heavy fighting.

properties.name: Tan Son Nhut air base
description: Saigon's airport and, from 1959 to 1973, one of the busiest military air bases in the world, home to the South Vietnamese air force and to the US command (MACV) headquarters, 'Pentagon East'. Its second 3,000 m runway was laid in 1967.

Three Viet Cong battalions attacked it at Tet in 1968; it was secured by the afternoon of 31 January. In April 1975 rockets and shells closed its runways. On 29 April two US Marines guarding the Defense Attaché Office compound were killed by a rocket, the last American ground deaths of the war, and the helicopter evacuation began from the compound's tennis courts and car parks.
